newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan MOF says no need for steps on stocks now.
newsitem.headline: Japan MOF says no need for steps on stocks now.

text.p: Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) does not see any need to take steps to boost Tokyo stocks at present ahead of the end of the current business year on March 31, the head of the ministry's securities bureau said on Thursday.

Bureau director-general Atsushi Nagano said, however, that the ministry would keep close watch on the situation in the stock market and the economy and take flexible steps if falls in share prices were hurting the economy.

Nagano told Reuters in an interview that his bureau would likely reach a conclusion on how to reform Japan's securities taxes in June, after receiving a proposal from an advisory panel expected by then on the nation's "Big Bang" financial reforms.
Senior figures in the ruling Liberal Democratic Party said on Wednesday they favoured abolishing the securities transaction tax.
Nagano said: "There is a gap between stock prices and the reality of the economy. The economy at the moment is heading upwards."
If falling share prices were undermining the economy, financial authorities must take a flexible attitude on economic management, he said.

Nagano said that speaking as head of the Finance Ministry's Securities Bureau, he believed securities taxes, including the securities transaction tax, must be discussed as part of Japan's Big Bang financial reforms, which would change the nation's securities market.
He said he believed the Big Bang reforms would in the long term help revitalise Japan's securities market, and that he planned to promote the reforms steadily.
He said the stock market had been focusing on negative aspects of the Big Bang reform plans, and this had resulted in selling of shares in the financial sector.
But he said the reforms in the long term would help reactivate the stock market.

He said financial institutions whose shares had been under selling pressure should themselves consider measures to attract investors and to ensure their credibility, such as restructuring and cutbacks in bad assets.
In the past when stock prices had tumbled, such as in the early 1990s, there had been fears that Japan's financial institutions might suffer if they cut dividends or even posted losses.
But experience in the past several years showed that such fears were unwarranted, he said.
Even if stock price levels on March 31, the end of the business year, hurt financial institutions' year-end statements, it should be seen as a transitory phenomenon.
The Big Bang reforms would create massive opportunities to be cultivated by securities houses, Nagano said.

While it was possible foreign companies might take over Japanese brokerages through mergers and acquisitions, the domestic firms would probably not be losers, as foreign firms came to Japan looking for business opportunities, he said.

Nagano said he hoped the advisory panel, the Securities and Exchange Council, would finalise its report by June so as to give an overall picture of the Big Bang reforms and procedures to promote them.
He said he wanted to send a package of legislation to an ordinary session of parliament starting in January next year to realise the Big Bang reforms.
